trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, Mount Baldy's summit and dune face remain closed to unguided hiking due to unstable, collapsing sand — the only way to reach the top is a scheduled ranger-led hike; the lower beach access route reopened to unguided visitors in June 2026.
trails.didYouKnow: Mount Baldy is a 'live' dune that migrates inland several feet a year, burying trees as it moves — a process visible in the park's 'ghost forest.'

trails.trailTip: Interpretive signs along the loop explain how dune plant communities change with distance from the lake, from bare sand to mature oak forest — reported loop length varies by source depending on which West Beach trail segments are combined, so check the trailhead map for your route.
trails.didYouKnow: The dune succession visible here helped inspire early 20th-century ecologist Henry Cowles' pioneering studies of plant succession.

trails.trailTip: The trail crosses a mix of wetland boardwalk, forest, and dune before reaching Lake Michigan — wear waterproof footwear for wet sections.
trails.didYouKnow: Cowles Bog is a National Natural Landmark named for Henry Cowles, whose research here helped found the science of ecology.

trails.trailTip: Bring binoculars — this flat boardwalk through a restored wetland is one of the park's best birding spots, especially during spring and fall migration.
trails.didYouKnow: The Great Marsh was once slated for drainage and development before restoration returned it to one of the largest interdunal wetlands on the Great Lakes.

trails.trailTip: A good low-key option for families — the loop climbs just enough to show off oak savanna and dune-ridge scenery without a long commitment.
trails.didYouKnow: Indiana Dunes protects one of the most biodiverse national parks in the system, packing over 1,100 plant species into a small footprint.

trails.trailTip: These older, more vegetated dune ridges see far fewer visitors than the lakefront trails — reported loop lengths vary across maps and sources, so confirm distance at the trailhead kiosk before setting out.
trails.didYouKnow: Tolleston Dunes are among the oldest dune ridges in the park, formed thousands of years before the active dunes along today's shoreline.

trails.trailTip: This out-and-back trail along the Little Calumet River is one of the best spring wildflower walks in the park, though it can be muddy after rain.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail is named for a great blue heron rookery once found nearby along the river corridor.

trails.trailTip: This loop through wetland and dune-ridge habitat is one of the quieter trails in the park — good footwear helps since sections can be sandy or damp.
trails.didYouKnow: Inland Marsh sits in a low area between old dune ridges, making it a haven for wetland-adapted plants and amphibians.

animals.whereToLook: Oak savanna where wild lupine grows, near West Beach and Tolleston Dunes
animals.viewingTip: Watch or photograph from the trail with a zoom lens — this federally endangered butterfly depends entirely on wild lupine, so stay on trail rather than stepping into lupine patches to get closer.
animals.didYouKnow: Karner blue caterpillars feed exclusively on wild lupine leaves, making the species' survival entirely tied to that one plant.

animals.whereToLook: Great Marsh and Inland Marsh during migration
animals.viewingTip: Scan the marshes with binoculars or a spotting scope during migration — cranes are easily flushed from feeding and roosting areas, so keep well back from any group you spot.
animals.didYouKnow: Sandhill cranes can live more than 20 years and often return to the same migratory stopover sites year after year.

animals.whereToLook: Wetland edges near Great Marsh and Cowles Bog
animals.viewingTip: As of 2026, the Eastern massasauga remains listed as a federally threatened species per the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — if you spot one, admire it from several feet away and never attempt to move, handle, or corner it; it will avoid you if given the space.
animals.didYouKnow: The Eastern massasauga is one of the smallest rattlesnakes in North America and relies on wetland habitat that has shrunk dramatically across its range.

animals.whereToLook: Forest and dune-ridge trails throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Watch quietly from the trail with binoculars, especially around dawn, and give does with fawns extra space in late spring.
animals.didYouKnow: White-tailed deer can leap fences and obstacles up to 8 feet high in a single bound.

animals.whereToLook: Great Marsh and other wetland trails
animals.viewingTip: Watch from the boardwalk or shoreline with binoculars — egrets hunt by standing motionless, and approaching too closely will flush them from good fishing spots.
animals.didYouKnow: Great egrets were hunted nearly to extinction in the early 1900s for their breeding plumes, used in the hat trade.

animals.whereToLook: Dune grasses and oak savanna; look for tracks rather than dens
animals.viewingTip: If you spot fox tracks or a den entrance in the dune grass, observe from a distance with binoculars and move on — resist lingering near a den, especially in spring when kits may be inside.
animals.didYouKnow: Red fox kits are born blind and stay in the den for about a month before venturing outside.

animals.whereToLook: Wetlands near Great Marsh and Inland Marsh
animals.viewingTip: Blanding's turtle is a species of conservation concern in Indiana — watch from a distance and never handle one, especially a female crossing a trail to nest; let her pass undisturbed.
animals.didYouKnow: You can recognize a Blanding's turtle by its bright yellow throat and chin, visible even from a distance.

animals.whereToLook: Dune ridges and open meadows along the lakeshore
animals.viewingTip: Watch and photograph monarchs nectaring on fall wildflowers rather than netting or handling them — they need to conserve energy for their journey to Mexico.
animals.didYouKnow: Migrating monarchs from this region can travel over 2,000 miles to overwintering sites in central Mexico.
